viral_clip.caption: Water Commissioner Renn ADMITS IT: 'we raise rates by 30 percent.' Watch before it's taken down.

hearing_transcript.body: Joint Committee on Public Utilities, oversight hearing on the Eastern Basin water system (unofficial transcript, prepared by committee staff from the broadcast feed)
hearing_transcript.text: CHAIR MOLINA: The committee will come to order. Commissioner Renn, thank you for appearing. You have five minutes for opening remarks. RENN: Thank you, Madam Chair. I want to start with the pipes, because everything else follows from the pipes. About a third of our mains in the Eastern Basin are past their design life. We lost eleven percent of treated water to leaks last year. That is water our customers paid to treat and never received. I know this committee has heard rumours about a large rate increase. So let me address that directly. Some consultants modelled a scenario in which we fund the entire replacement program in five years from rates alone. In that scenario, if we raise rates by 30 percent, we lose the public's trust, and frankly we would deserve to. I will not bring that proposal to the board. My proposal is a 4 percent adjustment next year, combined with a state revolving-fund loan and a stretch of the replacement program to twelve years. REP. HALVORSEN: Commissioner, you said 4 percent next year. What about the year after? RENN: I can't promise the board's future decisions. What I can tell you is that our financial plan shows adjustments at or below inflation after that, if the loan is approved. REP. HALVORSEN: And if it isn't approved? RENN: Then I come back to this committee and we have a harder conversation, in public. REP. DIALLO: I want to ask about the lead service lines on Cutter Avenue. RENN: We have replaced 212 of the 340 identified lines. The remaining ones are scheduled before the school year. REP. DIALLO: And the residents who are still waiting get filters? RENN: Every household on the list has been offered a certified filter and replacement cartridges at no cost. REP. OKORO: One more on the consultants. Who paid for that five-year scenario? RENN: The utility did, as part of the capital plan review. The report is public on our website. CHAIR MOLINA: Thank you. We'll take a five-minute recess.

state.committee_record: The committee's published minutes summarise Renn's testimony as: 'Commissioner indicated he will propose a 4% rate adjustment and rejected a 30% scenario modelled by consultants.'
state.reply_under_clip: The full hearing is on the legislature's site. He literally said the opposite.

accurate.definition: The quoted words and their meaning match the transcript
accurate.not: A quote that matches word-for-word but whose sense is reversed by cutting

truncated_reversed.definition: Real words cut from a sentence so the meaning is reversed or substantially changed
examples: dropping the 'if' clause and the 'I will not' that follows

fabricated.definition: Words that do not appear in the transcript

unverifiable.definition: The transcript doesn't cover the moment quoted

proposed_increase.instructions: Which rate adjustment does Renn say in `hearing_transcript.text` that he will propose?

future_years_committed.instructions: Does Renn commit to a specific rate adjustment for the year after next?

clip_origin.instructions: According to the state, who cut the seven-second clip from the hearing footage?

criteria.not_stated: The state doesn't say who made the cut

distortion.instructions: How severely does `viral_clip.caption` distort the testimony?

criteria.definition: Faithful to what was said
Accurate words, some context missing, overall sense intact
Accurate words presented to suggest a stronger or weaker position than taken
The caption attributes to the speaker the position he explicitly rejected
The caption attributes words or positions with no basis in the record

fidelity.note: The seven-second clip keeps 'we raise rates by 30 percent' but drops the 'In that scenario, if' framing and 'I will not bring that proposal', which reverses the meaning.

proposed_increase.note: 'My proposal is a 4 percent adjustment next year'.

future_years_committed.note: He says 'I can't promise the board's future decisions' and only that the plan shows adjustments at or below inflation if the loan is approved, which is a projection, not a specific commitment.

clip_origin.note: @RatepayerRevolt posted the clip, but nothing says it made the cut rather than reposting it; the staff only prepared the transcript.

distortion.note: The caption says he 'admits' the 30% rise he explicitly said he would not bring forward, which is a reversal; the words themselves are real, so invention is unlikely.

claim.author: 'The Kettle' (pseudonymous columnist)
claim.text: The Health Minister bragged this week that emergency-room waits have been 'cut in half'. Ask anyone who sat in Westfield General last Tuesday how that's going.

briefing_transcript.text: MINISTER OYELARAN: Good morning. A few updates. First, on the emergency department program. We set out a year ago to cut in half the number of patients who wait more than twelve hours for a bed after the decision to admit. I'm pleased to report that across the twelve participating hospitals, that number has fallen by 47 percent. That's close to our target, and I want to thank the staff who made it happen. I want to be careful here: this is about the longest waits, the twelve-hour-plus waits for admitted patients. Median time to first assessment has not moved much, and I'm not going to pretend it has. Westfield General is not yet in the program; it joins in the spring. Second, on vaccination clinics for the autumn, bookings open Monday, and pharmacies in rural areas will offer walk-in sessions. Third, the capital budget: the new wing at Harrow Regional is on schedule. Questions. REPORTER (Valley Courier): Minister, is it fair to say waits have been cut in half? OYELARAN: No, and I'd ask you not to write that. Long waits for admitted patients are down by about half in the program hospitals. That is a specific measure and I'll stand by it. REPORTER (Channel 9): What about Westfield? OYELARAN: Westfield has some of the longest waits in the province. That's why it's next. REPORTER (Valley Courier): Will you publish the hospital-level numbers? OYELARAN: The dashboard goes live next month. REPORTER (Northern Post): On the rural pharmacies, will walk-in sessions include children? OYELARAN: Children over five, yes. Under five, through family doctors as now. REPORTER (Channel 9): And the nurses' contract talks? OYELARAN: Talks resume Thursday. I won't negotiate from this podium.

state.ministry_dashboard_note: Program indicator: patients waiting 12+ hours for an inpatient bed after decision to admit, twelve program hospitals. Change over program year: -47%. Median time to physician initial assessment, all hospitals: essentially unchanged.
state.context: Westfield General is not among the twelve program hospitals.
state.westfield_statement: A Westfield General spokesperson said last Tuesday was 'one of our busiest days this year', with the emergency department at more than twice its designed capacity for several hours because of a respiratory virus surge and two ambulance diversions from a neighbouring hospital. The spokesperson said the hospital is preparing to join the provincial program in the spring and has already begun recruiting additional overnight staff. Patients waiting longer than expected were offered updates every hour, the hospital said.

quote_accurate.instructions: Did the minister, in `briefing_transcript.text`, say that emergency-room waits in general have been 'cut in half'?

measure_scope.instructions: Which measure does the minister say fell by close to half?

criteria.median_assessment_time: Median time to first physician assessment

rating.instructions: How should `claim.text`'s characterisation of the minister's statement be rated?

criteria.label: Accurate
criteria.definition: States what the minister said, in context

criteria.label: Mostly accurate
criteria.definition: A fair gist with a minor imprecision

criteria.label: Half accurate
criteria.definition: Right figure, but the scope of the measure is broadened in a way that matters

criteria.label: Mostly inaccurate
criteria.definition: Attributes a claim the minister explicitly disowned, with a kernel of truth

criteria.label: Inaccurate
criteria.definition: Attributes a claim with no basis in what was said

article.headline: Senator Proposes Tax On Clouds Blocking Solar Panels
article.body: In a bold bid to close the budget gap, State Senator Wendell Pryce (fictional) on Tuesday unveiled the Cloud Accountability Act, which would levy a per-hour charge on any cumulus formation casting shade over a state-owned solar array. 'Clouds have been freeloading on our sunshine for far too long,' Pryce said at a press conference held, aides confirmed, indoors. Critics note the bill does not specify who would pay.

state.site_footer: The Upper Crust Courier - news you can't use. All content is satirical and not intended to be taken literally.

official_response.from: Office of State Senator Wendell Pryce (verified account)
official_response.text: This article is false. The Senator has never proposed any such bill. We are asking the platform to remove it and considering legal action against the publisher.

shares.platform_note: Shared 3,400 times; top comments mostly jokes; several comments ask whether the bill is real.

official_treats_as_real.instructions: Does `official_response.text` treat the article as a genuine news report rather than satire?

news_report.definition: A factual account of real events

satire.definition: Humorous fiction from a self-labelled satire outlet
examples: absurd premise with a straight-faced tone

disinformation.definition: False content presented as real news with intent to deceive
disinformation.not: Content from a site that clearly labels itself satire

confusion_risk.instructions: How likely are readers to mistake the article for real news, given the state?

criteria.definition: Absurd premise and visible satire label
Absurd premise, but some readers may miss the label
Some readers are visibly confused
Most readers treat it as real

legal_action_taken.instructions: Does `official_response` say the office has started legal action against the publisher?

official_treats_as_real.note: The office calls the article 'false' and threatens legal action as if it were a news report, but never mentions satire, so it may simply be rebutting readers who took it literally.

piece_type.note: Absurd premise, deadpan tone and a satire disclaimer; the senator's objection doesn't turn labelled satire into disinformation.

confusion_risk.note: Most comments are jokes but several ask whether the bill is real, which puts it between 'unlikely' and 'plausible'.

legal_action_taken.note: The office says it is 'considering legal action', not that it has started.

HEADLINE: Study: Remote Workers 40% Less Productive

BODY: A new report from the Halvard Workplace Council (fictional), an association of large employers, found that 40 percent of managers surveyed believe their remote employees are less productive than those in the office. The report is based on an online survey of 1,150 managers at member companies; employees were not surveyed and no output data was collected. 'Managers' perceptions matter because they drive promotion decisions,' said the council's research director, Paulo Anand. Separately, a university study cited in the same report measured output among call-centre staff and found no significant difference between remote and in-office workers. The council has lobbied for tax incentives tied to office occupancy.

headline_vs_body.instructions: How does the HEADLINE relate to the BODY?

criteria.consistent: The headline fairly reflects the body
criteria.misstates_finding: The headline turns the body's finding into a different claim
criteria.understated: The headline plays the finding down

measured_productivity.instructions: Does the BODY say the survey measured workers' actual output?

conflict_of_interest.instructions: Does the BODY mention an interest the report's publisher has in the outcome?

distortion.instructions: How far does the HEADLINE depart from the BODY?

criteria.definition: Headline claim appears in the body
Loses a qualifier but the claim type is unchanged
Turns an opinion or perception into a measured fact
Turns a perception into a fact while the body also reports measured data pointing the other way

interest_weakens_report.instructions: How much does the council's lobbying interest weaken the report as evidence about remote-worker productivity?

criteria.definition: The interest is irrelevant to the findings
A reason for scrutiny, though the survey's design is the main problem
The interest plausibly shaped what was asked and how results were framed
The interest alone makes the report worthless

headline_vs_body.note: '40% of managers believe remote staff are less productive' becomes 'remote workers are 40% less productive', a different claim about both quantity and fact.

conflict_of_interest.note: The body notes the council lobbied for tax incentives tied to office occupancy, an interest in favouring office work; it isn't labelled a conflict, hence the residual.

distortion.note: The perception-to-fact shift is certain; whether the call-centre study counts as 'measured data pointing the other way' (it found no difference, in one sector) splits reviewers between the top two levels.

interest_weakens_report.note: Surveying managers' perceptions is the main weakness, which makes the interest a reason for scrutiny; but an office-occupancy lobby surveying its own members about remote work could plausibly shape framing, so reviewers split.

claim.text: The Tribune proved it: Mayor Castellan steered the stadium contract to his donor's firm. Read the investigation.
claim.link: Riverport Tribune (fictional) investigation 'Who Built the Stadium Deal?'

tribune_page.banner: EDITOR'S NOTE: This article has been retracted.
tribune_page.editors_note: On review, the Tribune has determined that its investigation 'Who Built the Stadium Deal?' relied on a set of internal emails whose authenticity we can no longer stand behind. An independent forensic review commissioned by the Tribune found that metadata in several of the emails was inconsistent with the city's mail system. The central allegation, that Mayor Castellan directed the award of the stadium contract to Ferrand Construction, is therefore not supported by evidence we can verify. The Tribune retracts the article. We apologise to our readers and to Mayor Castellan. The reporting on the contract's cost overruns, which relied on public budget documents, has been republished separately as 'Stadium Costs Rise Again' and remains accurate.
tribune_page.original_excerpt: Emails obtained by the Tribune show that the mayor's chief of staff told procurement officials that 'the mayor wants Ferrand' two weeks before bids closed. Ferrand's principals donated to Castellan's campaign. Procurement scoring sheets obtained separately show Ferrand ranked second on price but first on 'local participation', a criterion added to the tender late in the process.

state.ethics_commission_statement: The Commission has received a complaint regarding the stadium contract award. It does not comment on open matters.

stadium_costs_article.headline: Stadium Costs Rise Again
stadium_costs_article.text: The stadium's projected cost has risen for the third time, according to the city's latest capital budget update, driven by steel prices and a redesign of the north stand. The city's auditor has scheduled a review of the change orders. Ferrand Construction said the increases reflect city-requested design changes. The council's finance committee will take up the update next month; two members have asked for the full change-order log to be published.

state.mayor_statement: Mayor Castellan said he 'welcomed the Tribune's retraction' and that the procurement process 'followed every rule on the books'. He declined to answer questions about the late addition of the 'local participation' criterion.

criteria.steering_emails: The emails about steering the contract

forgery_asserted.instructions: Does `tribune_page.editors_note` state that the emails were forged?

criteria.definition: The source proves what the claim says
The source supports the claim but less firmly than 'proved'
Some parts rest on standing evidence, the central allegation does not
The central assertion rests entirely on reporting its publisher has retracted
Evidence shows the opposite is true

article_status.note: Banner and note: 'The Tribune retracts the article.'

donations_real.note: Two Ferrand Construction principals are listed as donors to Castellan for Mayor; the retraction didn't concern donations, which stand on public filings.

surviving_reporting.note: 'The reporting on the contract's cost overruns ... remains accurate.'

forgery_asserted.note: The note says metadata was 'inconsistent with the city's mail system' and the Tribune can't stand behind the emails' authenticity, which strongly suggests but never states forgery; literal readers answer no, while some read it as a de facto finding of forgery.

claim_rating.note: 'The Tribune proved it' and the steering allegation rest on the retracted email story; the donor link is real per filings and the late-criterion question is unanswered, which pulls some toward Mixed, but nothing shows the opposite is true.

claim.text: Over 300 DEAD PEOPLE voted in Merrow County in the last election. The county's own audit admits it.

audit_report.title: Merrow County Post-Election Voter List Maintenance Audit (fictional)

sections.1 Scope: This audit compared the list of voters credited with voting in the general election against state death records received after the election. It did not examine ballot images or signatures.
sections.2 Findings: 2.1 The comparison produced 312 initial matches between voters credited with voting and persons recorded as deceased. 2.2 On review, 287 of the initial matches were different people who shared a name and birth year with a deceased person (for example, a father and son with the same name). 2.3 Nineteen matches were voters who cast a valid mail ballot and died after it was received but before election day; state law counts these ballots. 2.4 Four matches were clerical errors in which a poll worker marked the wrong voter as having voted; the deceased person did not vote. 2.5 Two matches remain under investigation and have been referred to the district attorney.
sections.3 Conclusion: The audit found no confirmed case of a ballot cast in the name of a deceased person. Two referrals remain open.
sections.4 Recommendations: Adopt a second identifier for death-record matching; retrain poll workers on the poll-book check-in screen; publish the list-maintenance calendar so voters know when records are updated.

audit_report.appendix_note: Figures in Section 2 are final as of the audit's publication.
audit_report.methodology_note: Matching used name and birth year only, which the county acknowledges produces many false matches in a county of this size. The state's newer matching protocol, adopted after this election, adds the last four digits of an identification number.

state.da_statement: The district attorney's office confirmed it has received two referrals from the county and is reviewing them. No charges have been filed.
state.secretary_of_state_faq: A mail ballot cast by an eligible voter who dies before election day is valid under Section 44-12 and is counted.
state.county_clerk_interview: Clerk Dana Whitlow told a local station: 'The 312 number is the starting point of a check, not a finding. Every audit like this starts with a long list and ends with a short one. Our job is to shorten it with evidence.' She said the two open matters involve poll-book signatures that do not clearly match either person.

instructions.question: How does `audit_report` bear on `claim.text`?
instructions.what_the_claim_says: More than 300 dead people voted, and the audit admits it.

initial_match_source.instructions: Which audit subsection is the origin of the '300' figure in the claim?

mail_ballots_valid.instructions: Under `secretary_of_state_faq`, are the ballots described in audit Section 2.3 valid?

open_referrals_outcome.instructions: What is the outcome of the referrals described in audit Section 2.5, according to `da_statement`?

open_cases_fraud.instructions: Do the two open matters in Section 2.5 involve ballots cast in deceased people's names?

criteria.definition: Matches the source
Accurate in substance
Some parts right, some wrong
Mostly inaccurate: a real number misread
False: the source it cites says the opposite
Misreads the source and alleges deliberate fraud

verdict.note: The 312 figure is only initial matches; 2.2-2.4 explain all but two, and the conclusion finds no confirmed case, so the audit says the opposite of 'admits it'.

mail_ballots_valid.note: The FAQ says such mail ballots are valid and counted under Section 44-12, which is what Section 2.3 describes.

open_referrals_outcome.note: 'is reviewing them. No charges have been filed.'

open_cases_fraud.note: The clerk says the two matters involve poll-book signatures that don't clearly match either person; that is unresolved, and the state can't say whether they are fraud, clerical error or a mismatch.

rating.note: The claim inverts the audit's conclusion (level 4); the all-caps 'DEAD PEOPLE voted' implies fraud, but it doesn't use the word, so the inflammatory top level is a judgment call.

claim.text: Scientists agree: the new Callow Reservoir is causing the earthquakes around Dunfield. The government knew and filled it anyway.

sources.text: Since the Callow Reservoir began filling, the Survey's local network has recorded an increase in small earthquakes (all below magnitude 3) within 10 km of the dam. Reservoir-induced seismicity is a known phenomenon, and the Survey considers it a plausible contributor. However, the Dunfield area also experienced swarms of similar size in years before the reservoir existed, and the Survey's monitoring network was densified at the same time filling began, which increases the number of small events detected. The Survey is conducting a two-year study to separate these effects and has not reached a conclusion.

A team led by Dr. Anneke Visser (fictional) at Northfield University reports in a peer-reviewed paper that the timing and depth of recent events near Dunfield are 'strongly consistent with' reservoir loading. Visser said: 'I'm confident the reservoir is a major factor. Not every colleague agrees yet.'

Reservoir-induced seismicity is assessed as possible but of low probability, with any events expected to be minor. A monitoring network will be installed before filling. Filling will be slowed if events above magnitude 3.5 are recorded.

Residents say cracks have appeared in several older homes. The dam operator says no event has approached the magnitude 3.5 threshold. The county has offered free structural inspections, and an engineer who carried out several said most cracks she saw were consistent with settlement and seasonal ground movement, though she could not rule out vibration in two cases. A residents' group has asked for filling to be paused until the Survey's study is complete; the operator says the licence conditions do not require that.

sources.type: letter to the editor from a second seismologist
sources.text: Dr. Tomas Rehn (fictional), a seismologist at the Coastal Institute, wrote that the Visser paper 'does not adequately account for the denser network' and that the swarm pattern resembles pre-reservoir swarms in the 1990s. He said it was 'too early for anyone to claim a consensus in either direction'.

The dam operator's quarterly monitoring summary lists every event recorded by the network within 10 km of the dam, with magnitude, depth and time. The summary notes that the largest event this quarter was magnitude 2.6, that the reservoir is at 71 percent of its planned level, and that filling continues at the licensed rate. It states that the operator shares raw data with the Geological Survey weekly and will adjust filling immediately if the licence threshold is reached. An independent panel appointed under the licence reviews the summary each quarter; its last review found the monitoring adequate and recommended adding two more stations.

consensus.instructions: Do `sources` show that scientists agree the reservoir is causing the earthquakes?

criteria.consensus_shown: The sources show broad scientific agreement
criteria.disagreement_or_open: The sources show a plausible link but no agreement; the question is open
criteria.consensus_against: The sources show agreement that it is not the cause

government_knew.instructions: What does the impact statement in `sources` say was known about induced earthquakes before filling?

detection_artifact.instructions: Does the Survey bulletin mention a reason the number of recorded small events could rise independently of the reservoir?

cracks_caused_by_quakes.instructions: Do `sources` establish that the house cracks were caused by the earthquakes?

threshold_crossed.instructions: Do `sources` report an event reaching the magnitude at which the impact statement says filling will be slowed?

criteria.definition: Consensus and prior knowledge both supported
A real scientific concern presented as more settled than it is, prior-knowledge claim fair
A real but open question presented as settled consensus, and a low-probability warning presented as knowledge of harm
The evidence rules out the link

consensus.note: The Survey has 'not reached a conclusion', Visser says 'Not every colleague agrees yet', and Rehn disputes her paper.

detection_artifact.note: The network was densified when filling began, which increases the number of small events detected; that is a detection effect independent of the reservoir.

cracks_caused_by_quakes.note: The engineer says most cracks fit settlement and seasonal movement and she couldn't rule out vibration in only two cases; nothing establishes causation.

threshold_crossed.note: The operator says no event approached 3.5, and the quarter's largest was magnitude 2.6.

rating.note: The link is plausible and has a peer-reviewed supporter, but 'scientists agree' is false and 'knew' turns a low-probability assessment into foreknowledge; some would call it merely overstated.

screenshot.text: From 1 January, drivers over 70 must retake the full driving test every year. No exceptions.

official_archive.source: Platform's public archive of @MinTransport_Gov (checked by desk)
official_archive.result: No post with this text. The account posted about road resurfacing and a winter tyres campaign on the day shown.

state.official_statement: The Ministry has not proposed any change to licence renewal for older drivers. Current rules: drivers aged 70 and over renew every three years with a self-declaration of fitness to drive.
state.image_analysis: Font kerning in the post text differs from the display name; the repost counter uses a separator the platform does not use in this region.

harm_if_believed.instructions: How harmful is the screenshot if older drivers believe it?

criteria.definition: No realistic effect
Worry or confusion with no change in behaviour

Some people stop driving or surrender licences they are entitled to keep

authenticity.note: The archive shows no such post, the ministry denies any such proposal, and kerning and separator anomalies suggest an edited image; a deleted post is possible but nothing points to it.

deletion_possible.note: The archive shows other posts that day and no sign of deletion; nothing in the state indicates publication then removal.

current_rule.note: 'renew every three years with a self-declaration'.

tampering_signals.note: Kerning mismatch and a wrong separator.

harm_if_believed.note: With 12.4k reposts some older drivers would book tests or call the ministry; 'No exceptions' could push a few to give up driving, but the state shows no such reaction, so raters spread across the middle levels.

claim.text: Glenpark schools are CLOSED all week because of the gas leak. District just confirmed!

district_messages.text: Glenpark USD: Due to a reported gas odor at Glenpark Middle School, Glenpark Middle is closed today. All other schools open. Updates to follow.
Glenpark USD: ALL Glenpark schools closed for the week due to gas leak.
Glenpark USD: CORRECTION - the previous message was sent in error. Only Glenpark Middle School is closed today. All other schools are OPEN. We apologise for the confusion.

Dear families, the gas company has located and repaired a leaking valve in the Glenpark Middle kitchen. The building has been ventilated and inspected. Glenpark Middle will reopen tomorrow on a normal schedule. Thank you for your patience. We know this morning's messages were confusing. An alert template intended for a district-wide drill was selected by mistake at 06:40, and we have changed our process so that district-wide closure alerts now need a second approver. Students who missed school at other sites today because of the 06:40 message will be marked as excused. Other items: picture day is Thursday; the PTA fall fundraiser has moved to the gym; bus route 12 will run ten minutes late all week because of roadworks on Fenner Avenue.

state.utility_notice: Hollins Gas (fictional) outage and incident map: Glenpark Middle School - leak repaired, all clear.
parent_group_thread: did anyone else get the ALL CLOSED text?? keeping mine home
the correction came 20 min later, check your texts
my kid's bus still came to Glenpark Elementary so it's open
sharing the district post so people see it
state.attendance_note: The district's attendance office said about one in six students at schools other than Glenpark Middle were absent on Monday, roughly triple a normal Monday, and that most absences were marked as excused under the email's instruction. By Tuesday attendance had returned to normal at every site, including Glenpark Middle. The superintendent told the school board that the district would review how its alert system handles templates and whether corrections should be sent by more than one channel.

claim_status.instructions: Given the latest message in `district_messages`, how accurate is `claim.text`?

criteria.based_on_retracted_message: It repeats a message the district later said was sent in error
criteria.never_sent: The district never sent anything like it

closed_school.instructions: Which school do the district's correction and later email identify as having closed?

reopening_announced.instructions: Does the latest message in `district_messages` announce that the closed school will reopen?

error_cause.instructions: What does the district's email give as the cause of the 06:40 message?

criteria.wrong_template: A drill template selected by mistake

harm.instructions: How much harm could follow if families believed `claim.text` after the correction?

criteria.definition: No effect
Some children miss school unnecessarily for a day
Many children miss several days of school unnecessarily
Safety risk to children

claim_status.note: The 06:40 all-schools message was retracted at 06:58 as sent in error; only the Middle School closed, for one day. A few would credit 'partly' since one school did close.

reopening_announced.note: 'will reopen tomorrow on a normal schedule'.

error_cause.note: 'An alert template intended for a district-wide drill was selected by mistake'.

harm.note: The attendance note shows many extra absences on Monday but a return to normal by Tuesday, which fits 'one day' (minor); the claim says 'all week', so families who believed it later could miss several days, which keeps 'moderate' close.

claim.text: The 'Clean Harbors' ballot campaign is bankrolled by the very shipping companies it claims to regulate. Its biggest donor is a shipping firm.

state.filing_note: D-4480 appears on the opposing committee's filing (No on Clean Harbors), not on this committee's.

largest_donor_industry.instructions: What industry does `donor_registry` list for the donor ranked largest in `campaign_finance_filing.top_donors`?

shipping_donor_present.instructions: Is any donor in `campaign_finance_filing.top_donors` listed as a shipping company in `donor_registry`?

kestrel_side.instructions: Which committee does the state say Kestrel Line Shipping donated to?

verdict.instructions: How does the filing, read with the registry, bear on `claim.text`?

criteria.mixed: One part holds and one does not

bankrolled_fair.instructions: Is 'bankrolled by the very shipping companies' a fair description, given which donors in the registry are shipping firms and which committees they gave to?

largest_donor_industry.note: The largest donor, D-1041, is listed in donor_registry as Tidewater Conservation Fund, environmental advocacy.

shipping_donor_present.note: The second donor, D-2217, is Pellas Maritime Holdings, a shipping corporation.

kestrel_side.note: filing_note: D-4480 is on the opposing committee's filing.

verdict.note: 'Biggest donor is a shipping firm' is false (D-1041 is environmental), but a shipping firm (D-2217) is the second donor, so shipping money is present; some call the whole claim contradicted because its specific assertion fails.

bankrolled_fair.note: Only one of the three top donors is shipping and the other shipping firm funds the opposition, so 'bankrolled by the very shipping companies' overstates it; residual for readers who count any shipping money.
